newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION - Louthean on Australian Mining: Locals look into Africa.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Louthean on Australian Mining: Locals look into Africa.

text.p: *By Ross Louthean
Who is benefiting from the morass created by the Native Title land claims and other negatives affecting the process of mineral exploration in Australia?
One answer could be Qantas, South African Airways, Air Zimbabwe and Singapore Airlines, and any other international airline that carries Australians into Africa.

On any given day for a Johannesburg-bound flight the Qantas lounge at Perth international airport will have local geologists, mining executives and mining analysts. They are going to South Africa, Tanzania, Kenya, Botswana, the West African nations and just about everywhere bar Liberia and Rwanda.
The magnet of Africa has not been sudden but it has been profound to the point that it must now be the prime foreign region where Australians are spending exploration and development dollars.

A good illustration of this was the recent Investment in African Mining Conference in Cape Town which attracted more than 900 delegates, of which at least 150 were Australian and about another 300 were Canadians.

The Aussie mix there was interesting -- from well established African explorers, juniors with a toehold in the continent or seeking one, a few majors and several gold producers looking for new fields.

As with any conference the networking was important and the huddles were not just Australians talking to Ministers and representatives of African nations but Australians in earnest conversation with Canadians.
There lies another trend!

In the past two years there has been a steady trek of Australians to Canada, notably the venture capital centre of Vancouver for junior companies. The home front has not been a good place for high risk juniors to raise capital for a listing or to produce a solidy-backed prospectus for a new capital raising.
What many failed to achieve visiting Australian stockbrokers in up to three capital cities has been achieved in Vancouver in an hour.

While observers now believe the exercises of dual listing has not been a great success, owing to the differing demands of compliance and reporting standards there have been some interesting variations.

General Gold Resources NL which was finding it difficult to raise more capital domestically for the next development stage on its project in Mauritania in West Africa, solved the problem by selling the project to Canadian company Solomon Resources Ltd .
This gave General Gold a control position in Solomon and part of this deal was that Solomon undertakes to raise $C10 million to fund its newly acquired African projects.
There are a host of mechanisms applied and being applied to raise funds outside of Australia.

This adds to the growing concern of red tape and the Aboriginal industry (made up in part of assignment-seeking legal firms) putting new exploration areas in Australia in limbo. Now through the expensive and cumbersome demands of listing and the perceived lack of flexibility within the Australian Stock Exchange, this has opened the door of the Vancouver Stock Exchange and "second board" style exchanges in Calgary and Montreal to lure the Australians.

This new trend has just received a setback through the Bre-X Minerals disaster where a high flying stock with a purportedly world class gold discovery at Busang in Indonesia has given Canadians their biggest lesson in the laws of sharemarket gravity.

One repercussion has already been felt in Australia. Canadian company Yamana Resources has pulled the pin on a venture with Union Mining which has projects in Papua New Guinea. Other companies have also heard negatives from nervous Canadian broking houses, undoubtedly exposed to Bre-X or to other companies affected by the fall out.

However, should this pass with limited damage then Canada may continue to be mecca for Australian companies, well regarded for their entrepreneurial nous, prospects and, if Austrlian listed, low price-earnings ratios -- something which Bre-X showed Canadian stocks lack.

Several Australian companies, listed or unlisted, told this writer prior to the Bre-X crash that they saw their future as expanding their portfolios by moving into Africa (and probably make these their prime areas) and funding this through Canadian markets -- in some cases with funds derived from the United States -- and eventually having a Canadian bourse as its home base.
For companies more intent on keeping the home fires burning while dealing with Africa one of the options has been to link up with the big South African mining houses and with North American miners.

Examples of this have been Kimberley Diamond Company NL's link with JCI Ltd which facilitated the move into Lone Star Exploration NL which has the Awak Mas project in Indonesia; Equinox Resources NL's joint venture with Anglo American Corporation to explore for massive copper-gold deposits in southern Africa; Moonstone Diamond Corporation NL's marine diamond joint venture with Cape Town-based Benguala Concessions Ltd off South Africa's Namaqualand coast; Camelot Resources NL's joint venture with Teck Corporation of the U.S. and Anglo American's 14.9 percent take up of Tanganyika Gold NL with which it has a joint venture in Tanzania.

Apart from the diverse opportunities throughout most of Africa, helped by the fact that there has been a strong growth in political stability and exploration and taxation incentives that put Australia in the Ozarks, there are also good opportunities for Australians inthe heartland of South African mining.

There has been an "unbundling" of the handful of mega mining houses which virtually controlled every facet and every prospect in the country. This has seen the Mandela ANC Government now demanding these mining houses to shed long-term mineral properties and while this now allows new black African companies to take up areas they and South Africa lack entrepreneurs. Starting new projects from scratch or on a shoestring is something Australians have mastered.
*Ross Louthean is editor of Paydirt and Gold Mining Journal and publisher of the new Australian Mines Handbook.
